full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 230

XinMou Shipping Co., Ltd. v. China JiMou International Cooperation Co., Ltd. — dispute over maritime cargo transport contract

(Discussed and adopted by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on November 25, 2024)

Keywords civil; maritime cargo transport contract; contractual shipper; actual shipper; non-delivery at destination port; liability for compensation

Ruling Gist

According to Article 42 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China, a shipper includes both the contractual shipper who enters into a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier and the actual shipper who delivers the goods to the carrier. Where the consignee does not claim delivery of the goods or exercise other rights from the carrier, the expenses and risks arising from non-delivery at the destination port shall be borne by the contractual shipper, who is a party to the maritime cargo transport contract, and the actual shipper shall not be liable for compensation therefor.

Basic Facts

XinMou Shipping Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as XinMou Shipping) alleged: China JiMou International Cooperation Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as China JiMou International) booked space with it for the shipment of a batch of goods, totaling 26 40-foot containers, from Tianjin Xingang, China to Laem Chabang Port, Thailand, and XinMou Shipping accepted the booking. On July 2, 2018, the goods in question were loaded on board the vessel "C Mou" on voyage 031S, and XinMou Shipping issued an order bill of lading, with China JiMou International recorded as the shipper on the bill of lading. The goods arrived at the destination port on July 14, 2018, but were never collected, resulting in losses such as container detention charges and terminal storage charges. Therefore, XinMou Shipping sought an order for China JiMou International to compensate for these losses and to return the containers.

China JiMou International argued: It was not the contractual shipper of the maritime cargo transport contract in question, but only the actual shipper. It had delivered the goods in accordance with the trade contract it entered into with HaiMou Enterprise Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as HaiMou Company), and had submitted all negotiation documents including the bill of lading to the bank and received payment. Thereafter, it did not have any rights over the goods and should not bear any liability. China JiMou International had no fault in the non-delivery at the destination port. Moreover, since China JiMou International did not actually possess the containers in question, XinMou Shipping's request for the return of the containers had no legal basis.

The court found upon trial: In March 2018, HaiMou Company and China JiMou International entered into a trade contract, stipulating that HaiMou Company would purchase a batch of goods (seamless steel pipes) from China JiMou International, with the port of loading being Tianjin Xingang, China, the port of discharge being Laem Chabang Port, Thailand, and the payment term being an irrevocable sight letter of credit. To perform this trade contract, HaiMou Company entered into a container agency agreement with Tianjin ShengMou International Logistics Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as ShengMou Company) on May 11, 2018, entrusting ShengMou Company to provide freight forwarding services for the goods. After accepting the entrustment, ShengMou Company entrusted Tianjin FuMou International Freight Forwarding Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as FuMou Company) to book space, and FuMou Company further booked space with XinMou Shipping. After accepting the booking, XinMou Shipping loaded the goods contained in 26 40-foot containers on board and shipped them on July 2, 2018. The transaction was concluded on FOB (Free On Board) price terms, whereby the buyer HaiMou Company was responsible for contracting for the carriage of the goods, and the seller China JiMou International was responsible for delivering the goods on board the vessel designated by the buyer. The order bill of lading in question recorded China JiMou International as the shipper, the consignee to order, XinMou Shipping as the carrier, and HaiMou Company as the notify party. XinMou Shipping collected freight and related charges through the booking company. On July 14, 2018, the goods arrived at the destination port, Laem Chabang Port, Thailand, and were discharged. As of the time of trial, the goods remained uncollected at the destination port.

It was further found that China JiMou International had received the full payment by presenting the bill of lading to the issuing bank for negotiation.

Judgment

The Tianjin Maritime Court rendered a civil judgment (2019) Jin 72 Min Chu No. 1012 on December 26, 2019, dismissing all claims of the plaintiff, XinMou Shipping Co., Ltd. After the judgment of first instance was pronounced, XinMou Shipping appealed. The Tianjin High People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2020) Jin Min Zhong No. 466 on November 27, 2020, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. After the second-instance judgment was pronounced, XinMou Shipping applied for retrial. The Supreme People's Court rendered a civil ruling (2021) Zui Gao Fa Min Shen No. 5588 on December 9, 2021, rejecting XinMou Shipping's application for retrial.

Reasoning

The obligation of the carrier under a contract of carriage of goods by sea is to transport the goods safely to the destination port and complete delivery. After the goods arrive at the destination port, the consignee shall timely take delivery of the goods. Where the consignee does not claim delivery of the goods or exercise other rights from the carrier, and losses are caused to the carrier due to non-delivery at the destination port, the shipper shall bear liability for compensation. According to Article 42, item (3) of the Maritime Code, shippers include two types: one is "the person who, or on whose behalf, enters into a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier, either in the person's own name or through another person," i.e., the contractual shipper; the other is "the person who, or on whose behalf, delivers the goods to the carrier in connection with the contract of carriage of goods by sea, either in the person's own name or through another person," i.e., the actual shipper. The contractual shipper is the person who enters into the contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier and is responsible for ensuring that the goods can be collected by the consignee at the destination port, and bears liability for compensation for economic losses arising from non-delivery at the destination port. In contrast, the actual shipper is not the person who enters into the contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier, but merely the person who delivers the goods to the carrier; the consignee is not designated by the actual shipper, and therefore the actual shipper should not bear liability for compensation for economic losses arising from non-delivery at the destination port.

In this case, although the bill of lading in question recorded China JiMou International as the shipper, the maritime cargo transport contract in question was entered into by HaiMou Company through another person on its behalf with XinMou Shipping, the freight was paid by HaiMou Company through another person to XinMou Shipping, and the goods were delivered by China JiMou International to XinMou Shipping. It can be seen that China JiMou International meets the legal characteristics of an actual shipper under Article 42, item (3) of the Maritime Code, rather than a contractual shipper. As the goods were not collected at the destination port, and in accordance with the principle of privity of contract, where there is no transport contract relationship between China JiMou International and XinMou Shipping, and the bill of lading in question had been transferred under the letter of credit, with China JiMou International not holding nor claiming any rights under the bill of lading, China JiMou International is not required to bear liability for compensation to XinMou Shipping for losses arising from non-delivery at the destination port. The relevant expenses and risks shall be borne by the contractual shipper. At the same time, China JiMou International did not possess or control the containers in question, and therefore is not required to bear the obligation to return the containers.
